intro-1: Pairing buddy, or Pair for short, is a pair programmer that sits beside you in Neovim.
intro-2: It watches while you work, and speaks only when something matters.
intro-3: Its words appear where you are already looking.
intro-4: And it changes your code only when you hand it the wheel. This tutorial shows each of these, one at a time.
screen-card: First, the screen you will see in every scene. Watch the four labelled areas.
screen-1: On the left is Neovim, with your code.
screen-2: Under it is your terminal, where you run commands.
screen-3: On the right is Pair’s chat. It keeps a record of what Pair says, and you can type to it.
screen-4: And along the bottom, the statusline shows what Pair is doing right now.
screen-sum: Your code, your terminal, the chat, and the statusline. Pair uses all four.
install-card: Pair is a Neovim plugin and a small program that runs in the background, the daemon. Watch the last lines of each command.
install-1: One npm command installs it, straight from GitHub.
install-2: Then pair setup writes a config file from the example, offers a login, and starts the daemon as a service, so it runs from now on.
install-3: Last, it says what to add to Neovim: the plugin, for lazy dot nvim, or any plugin manager.
install-sum: Two commands: Pair is installed, and its daemon runs as a service.
doctor-card: Pair needs a model: a server on your machine, or a cloud provider with a key. Watch the ticks pair doctor prints.
doctor-1: The config names one model for both jobs. This tutorial uses DeepSeek, in the cloud.
doctor-2: Pair auth stores the key, in a file only you can read. It never prints it.
doctor-3: Then pair doctor checks every part: the service, the daemon, the plugin in Neovim, the sandbox for commands, and the model itself.
doctor-4: It asks the model a question, times the answer, and checks that it thinks. A cross, instead of a tick, would name the fix.
doctor-sum: A config, a key, and pair doctor: every part checked before you start.
roles-1: Two models share the work. The Watcher is small and fast. It scores every moment from zero to ten: is this worth a word?
roles-2: Only high scores reach the Partner. It thinks first, reads your code, and writes what Pair says. One model can play both parts.
roles-3: The Partner works in one of three roles, and the statusline always says which.
roles-4: Navigator is the default. It watches, and points at code.
roles-5: Scout runs commands for you, in a pane of its own, inside a sandbox.
roles-6: And Driver types one change into your buffer, then gives the wheel back.
scout-card: You want to know why a test fails, without digging yourself. Watch the chat, and the pane that opens at the bottom.
scout-1: In the chat, slash scout switches Pair to the Scout role.
scout-2: Then you ask your question, in plain words.
scout-3: Pair’s own pane opens at the bottom. Scout runs the test there, and searches the code. Every command is typed where you can see it, in a sandbox: only the project is writable, and there is no network.
scout-4: The answer comes back in the chat: the greater-or-equal on line thirty-five drops the retry that fits exactly.
scout-sum: You asked once; Scout ran the test in plain sight and answered in the chat.
wrong-turn-card: A test fails, and you start fixing the wrong file. Watch the margin, under the line you change.
wrong-turn-1: In your terminal, the delivery test fails: it wants five attempts, and gets four.
wrong-turn-2: You guess the backoff is wrong, and change the shift on line twenty.
wrong-turn-3: Pair saw the red test, and an edit in a file the failure doesn’t name. The Watcher scores that a wrong turn, worth a word.
wrong-turn-4: So the Partner reads the code, and speaks once, under the line you changed. The cause is the greater-or-equal in worker dot go.
wrong-turn-5: Alt J goes where it points. Your cursor never moves by itself.
wrong-turn-sum: Pair spoke once, where you were looking, and pointed at the real cause.
notes-card: You are writing a design note, not code yet. Watch the margin of the note.
notes-1: You finish a sentence about dead letters, and stop to think.
notes-2: When you stop, Pair reads the whole note, and the code it names.
notes-3: Its notes land in the margin, each with a sign. A question mark is a question the note leaves open.
notes-4: The not-equal sign marks two lines that can’t both be true: five attempts here, six there.
notes-5: The arrow says what the code really does. Here, the note is wrong about worker dot go.
notes-6: Nothing in the note changed. The marks are only in the margin.
notes-7: When you are ready to build, Pair tasks lists the work the note asks for. Nothing is added until you say so.
notes-sum: Pair read the note like a colleague: questions, contradictions, facts, in the margin.
blank-page-card: An empty folder, and an idea. No code yet. Watch the note, under your last line.
blank-page-1: Pair new, and one sentence: what you want to try.
blank-page-2: Pair starts a note with your idea, and asks one question under it.
blank-page-3: You answer on the next line, in a few words.
blank-page-4: Each answer brings the next question, one at a time. Here, how the stall happens.
blank-page-5: And whether to cap the steps. Three short answers are enough.
blank-page-6: Then Pair suggests a first slice, dimmed, under your answers: two files, what they print, what to poke at, and what to leave out for now.
blank-page-7: Alt Y takes it into the note. Nothing is written to disk until you save.
blank-page-sum: Three questions, three short answers, and a first slice small enough to start.
hand-over-card: You want the edge cases of a table test written, and you’d rather watch. Watch your code, and the statusline.
hand-over-1: You hand over with Pair drive, and say what you want.
hand-over-2: Pair is the Driver now. The statusline says it has the wheel. It reads the test and the code first.
hand-over-3: Then it types, into your buffer, where you can see every line arrive.
hand-over-4: It runs the tests on the unsaved buffer, in its own pane at the bottom, and hands the wheel back with a short note.
hand-over-5: Nothing is saved yet. U takes the whole change away in one step, and control R brings it back.
hand-over-sum: Pair typed one change in plain sight, tested it, and gave the wheel back.
voice-card: Your hands are on the code, and a question comes up. Watch the line under your cursor.
voice-1: Hold Alt T, and ask out loud. The meter shows Pair hears you.
voice-2: Let go, and whisper dot c p p writes down what it heard, on your own machine. That is your question, under your line.
voice-3: Then Pair answers in the same place, and points at line thirty-five. Alt J would go there.
voice-sum: You asked out loud, and the answer came where you were looking. Voice is off until you set it up.
herdr-1: Pair works with or without herdr, the terminal workspace for coding agents.
herdr-2: Without it, one Neovim holds everything. Pair chat opens the chat, and Pair’s own pane is a terminal at the bottom.
herdr-3: Every scene you just saw ran this way.
herdr-4: With herdr, the chat and Pair’s pane are panes of their own. Pair also sees your other agents on herdr’s board, and terminals outside Neovim.
herdr-5: Either way, it is the same Pair, with the same keys.
keys-1: Here are the keys to remember. Alt J goes where Pair points, and Alt Y takes its suggested change. Alt question mark explains the idea behind its words. Pair drive hands over one change, U undoes it, and any key takes the wheel back. Hold Alt T to ask out loud, and run pair doctor whenever something seems off.
keys-2: Pairing buddy is on GitHub. Happy pairing.
tests-card: You fix one line, and a test somewhere else breaks. Watch the statusline, then the ghost text.
tests-1: Each time you save, Pair runs your tests, in its own pane at the bottom. The delivery test is red.
tests-2: You fix the check on line thirty-five, from greater-or-equal to greater, and save again.
tests-3: Delivery passes now, but a queue test that passed before now fails. That is a regression, and the Watcher scores it high.
tests-4: Pair says why, under your line: the queue’s lease runs out just as the last attempt starts.
tests-5: Alt J goes to its fix, in queue dot go. The ghost text shows the old line struck through, and the new one under it. Nothing has changed yet.
tests-6: Alt Y takes it into your buffer. You save, the tests run again, and they pass.
tests-sum: Pair ran the tests you might skip, caught a regression, and showed its fix before you took it.
take-back-card: Pair is typing, and you change your mind. Watch the lines it types, and the chat.
take-back-3: You press any key. The typing stops, and what it typed is gone, as if it never started.
take-back-4: The chat says you have the wheel back, and Pair is the Navigator again.
take-back-sum: Any key takes the wheel back, and nothing Pair typed stays behind.
x-open-1: Pairing buddy is an AI pair programmer for Neovim. Here are three moments from an ordinary day.
x-margin-card: You edit the wrong file while a test is red. Watch the margin.
x-margin-2: Pair speaks once, under your line. The real cause is in worker dot go.
x-margin-sum: One remark, in the right place.
x-tests-card: You fix one line, and save. Watch the statusline, then the ghost text.
x-tests-1: Pair runs your tests on every save.
x-tests-2: A test that passed before now fails.
x-tests-3: Alt J shows Pair’s fix as ghost text: the old line struck through, the new one under it.
x-tests-4: Alt Y takes it. Save, and it’s green.
x-tests-sum: It runs the tests you would skip.
x-drive-card: You hand Pair the wheel for one change. Watch your code.
x-drive-1: Pair drive, and say what you want.
x-drive-2: It types where you can see it, tests the unsaved buffer, and hands back.
x-drive-3: U undoes it all, in one step.
x-drive-sum: It touches your code only when you hand it the wheel.
x-end-1: Pairing buddy. The full tutorial, the docs and the code are on GitHub.
